passages.t: Skin for skin: the second test
passages.happening:
On another day the heavenly beings come before the LORD, and Satan comes with them. The LORD asks again, “Have you considered My servant Job?” (verse 3), and adds, “He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause” (verse 3).

“Skin for skin!” Satan replies. “A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life” (verse 4). Strike his flesh and bones, he says, and Job will curse God to his face.

“Very well,” the LORD says. “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life” (verse 6). Satan goes out and strikes Job with terrible boils ‘from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head’ (verse 7). ‘And Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sat among the ashes’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The heavenly scene repeats chapter 1 almost word for word, so the differences stand out. The LORD adds a new line: Job still holds on to his integrity, tummah, a word found in Job more than anywhere else. And the LORD uses the accuser's own word from 1:9, chinnam, without cause. The reader is told twice that Job's suffering has no cause in Job.

‘Skin for skin’ is an obscure saying, but its point is clear. People will give up anything to save themselves. The accuser says Job has only lost what was outside him. Touch his body, and his faith will go.

The disease is not described in medical terms. The word for the sores is the one used of the boils in Egypt (Exodus 9:9) and of the disease in Deuteronomy 28:35 that covers a person from foot to head. Attempts to name a modern diagnosis are guesswork.

The ashes were a place of mourning and of exclusion. Outside many ancient towns lay a dump where refuse was burned, and the diseased and the outcast sat there. The greatest man of the East now sits where the lowest sit, scraping himself with a broken piece of a pot.
passages.later: The same sores stand among the law's warnings to Israel, boils ‘from the soles of your feet to the top of your head’ (Deuteronomy 28:35). In Job they fall on a man God himself calls blameless.
passages.asks: Job lost his health as well as his household, and he sat where outcasts sat. Ask who sits in the ashes near you, out of sight, in illness or shame. And ask whether you have ever measured someone's faith by how well things were going for them.

passages.happening:
Then Job's wife speaks: “Do you still retain your integrity? Curse God and die!” (verse 9).

“You speak as a foolish woman speaks,” he told her. “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” (verse 10).

‘In all this, Job did not sin in what he said’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
She speaks one sentence, and he answers with one question. Her question repeats the LORD's own word from verse 3: integrity. Her advice, curse God, is what the accuser predicted, now in the mouth of the person closest to Job. The Hebrew uses the opposite word, by a reverent turn of speech that avoids writing the words curse God, but its meaning is plain.

Job does not call her a fool. He says she speaks as a foolish woman speaks. The word, naval, means more than unintelligent. It describes someone who acts as though God does not matter. Job says her advice sounds like that, not that she is that.

His answer, “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” (verse 10), sums up the challenge of the book.

The narrator's verdict changes slightly from 1:22. Job did not sin ‘in what he said’, literally with his lips. Some interpreters hear a hint that turmoil is beginning inside him. Others think the phrase simply marks his words as blameless.
passages.later: The Hebrew word Job uses for adversity covers both moral evil and calamity. Isaiah uses it when the LORD says, “I bring prosperity and create calamity” (Isaiah 45:7). She disappears from the story, though Job speaks of her once more, in his loneliness (19:17).
passages.hard:
Is Job's wife wicked, or a grieving mother?

Many interpreters in the church's history read her harshly, as the accuser's tool, since she urges Job to do exactly what the accuser predicted. But she had lost the same ten children and the same livelihood, and now she was watching her husband waste away. Many readers hear in her words despair rather than malice, perhaps even a wish that his suffering would end.

Job's reply is firm but not contemptuous. The ancient Greek translation expands her speech into a lament for her own losses and wanderings, which shows that early readers also felt the weight of her grief. Both readings take her words seriously. The more compassionate one also takes her suffering seriously.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job refused to curse God, and he did not despise his wife. Ask how you answer someone whose grief has turned to bitterness: with contempt, or with firmness and patience. And ask whether you would say what Job said in verse 10, and what it would cost you to mean it.

passages.t: Three friends, and seven days of silence
passages.happening:
Job's three friends hear about his trouble: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. ‘Each of them came from his home, and they met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him’ (verse 11).

When they see him from a distance, they can barely recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes and throw dust in the air over their heads.

‘Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The friends come from places with Edomite and Arabian connections. Teman was a clan and region of Edom, named for a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11), and Edom was known for its wise men. Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Naamah has not been identified with certainty. That they arrange to meet suggests some time had passed since Job's disasters.

They come to comfort him, nacham, a word that will return with irony when Job calls them ‘miserable comforters’ (16:2). But their first comfort is silent presence.

Weeping aloud, tearing robes and throwing dust over the head were the customs of grief. Sitting with a mourner for seven days recalls the seven days of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10), a practice that lives on in the Jewish custom of shiva, from the Hebrew word for seven. Whatever their later failures, the friends' first act is compassion, and it is the best thing they do.
passages.later: Paul makes the friends' first week a command for every church: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).
passages.asks: The friends did their best work when they said nothing. Ask whether you are quick to explain someone else's pain. And ask whether you could sit with a grieving friend for an hour, or a day, without trying to fix it.
